motions.item_title: Councillor N. Salonen, Re: Regional Councillor Conference Budget
motions.text: Whereas the Region of Waterloo currently provides an uncapped conference and professional development budget for Members of Council, permitting reimbursement for up to three (3) conferences per Councillor per year; and Whereas a review of historical expenditures from 2018–2025 shows that the average cost of the most expensive annual conference attended by Councillors is $3,072, with costs in recent years trending closer to $3,500; and Whereas fiscal responsibility, prudent budgeting, and alignment with resident expectations require Council to demonstrate leadership in containing discretionary spending; and Whereas ensuring access to at least one high-quality learning or conference opportunity per year continues to support Council’s effectiveness, professional growth, and informed decision-making; and Whereas the Regional Chair, as Head of Council and representative for the Region of Waterloo, is required to attend multiple provincial and national conferences annually as part of intergovernmental responsibilities and regional advocacy efforts; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT: The Councillor conference and professional development allocation be amended to permit coverage for up to one (1) conference per Councillor per calendar year; and A maximum annual reimbursement limit of $3,500 per Councillor be established for conferences and professional development expenses, inclusive of registration, travel, accommodation, and related eligible costs; and The Regional Chair’s current allocation permitting up to three (3) conferences per year remain unchanged, recognizing the Chair’s expanded responsibilities and required participation in intergovernmental forums; and Staff be directed to bring back, no later than the March 2026 Committee cycle, a proposed policy update to reflect these budget decisions, including recommended wording to incorporate professional development into the policy and clarify how Double Direct elected officials may access conference and professional development funding while attending in the capacity of the office to which they were elected. This policy update shall be prepared following the passage of the 2026 Budget, with no impact on the budget decision itself.

motions.item_title: Councillor N. Salonen, Re: Waterloo Region Health Network Special Levy
motions.text: Whereas the Province of Ontario requires municipalities to contribute a local share toward major hospital capital projects, and the forthcoming Waterloo Region Health Network (WRHN) hospital project is anticipated to require one of the largest municipal contributions in the Region’s history; Whereas early estimates indicate that the Region’s required local share will be in the multiple hundreds of millions, and this magnitude of investment will require long-term, disciplined financial planning; Whereas the Region of Waterloo must balance many competing and necessary capital priorities, and failing to begin reserving funds now would require significant future tax impacts or the deferral of other essential regional projects; Whereas establishing a dedicated, interest-bearing reserve fund enables the Region to gradually and responsibly accumulate contributions over multiple budget cycles, mitigating the need for sudden or unsustainable fiscal adjustments once the provincial approval process is finalized; Therefore be it resolved that: Council establish a Special Hospital Local Share Levy equivalent to 0.5% of the annual tax-supported budget, beginning in the 2026 fiscal year. All revenues collected through this Special Levy be directed to a newly created “Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund,” to be invested in accordance with the Region’s investment policy to allow funds to grow over time. The Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund be used exclusively for the municipal local share contribution required for the future WRHN hospital project and subsequently agreed upon Cambridge Hospital projects. Staff be directed to report annually during the budget process on the balance, growth, and projected trajectory of the Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund to ensure transparency and enable long-term planning. That staff bring back before budget 2027 the local share amount confirmed by the Province to Council, or continued suggestion for 2027 levy amount.

motions.item_title: Councillor B. Vrbanovic, Police Budget
motions.text: Whereas the 2026 Waterloo Region Police Service proposed operating budget reflects the increased operational policing needs expressed by our growing community; And whereas the Waterloo Region Police Service (WRPS), under contract at the present time with the Region of Waterloo as the PSAP for emergency services within Waterloo region has identified the need for a new, modern communications centre to serve our community and their contractual partners; And whereas the WRPS has expressed an ambition to build a shared services centre that goes beyond their mandate as a PSAP and as a police service; And whereas as of this date no potential partners have come forward with a signed agreement to be part of an over-sized new facility, and it is highly unlikely that all three emergency services would engage in this partnership in any foreseeable future; Be It Resolved: That Region of Waterloo Council not approve the 2026 Waterloo Regional Police Service Capital Budget as presented; And further that Region of Waterloo staff send the proposed budget to the WRPS and be directed to work with the Waterloo Region Police Service to bring back a capital budget for consideration that reduces the overall capital ask by WRPS to something that is both more affordable and considers overall debt load by Region of Waterloo taxpayers when considering other critical investments and needed debt for the region and area municipalities including for affordable housing, water system improvements, local share of the new hospital, transit expansion, infrastructure renewal and more; And further that the Region of Waterloo Council approve the proposed 2026 WRPS Operating budget, recognizing that the operating budget begins to address key community public safety needs being called for by our growing community.

motions.item_title: Councillor C. James, Re: Canada-Wide Early Learning Child Care Advocacy
motions.text: Whereas the Region of Waterloo, as the provincially designated Service System Manager for early learning and childcare, is responsible for planning, allocating, and managing licensed child care growth in accordance with provincial requirements; and Whereas demand for childcare significantly exceeds the supply of provincially funded spaces, with over 14,000 children currently on the waitlist, demonstrating a critical shortfall in affordable, high-quality childcare for families in our rapidly growing community; and Whereas notwithstanding the provincially funded junior kindergarten program, the provincial government’s contributions to the CWELCC program fall far short of the federal contribution despite this being a provincial responsibility. Whereas Waterloo Region is a unique and rapidly growing community projected to reach one million residents , and this growth includes infants, toddlers, and young children, yet planning and funding models often view growth predominantly through an adult lens, overlooking that children are essential contributors to the present and future health and vibrancy of our communities; and Whereas Waterloo Region has been underfunded by the Province of Ontario, creating limitations on the Region’s ability to support children, families, and operators, despite high need and sustained population growth; and Whereas childcare access is an equity issue, disproportionately impacting women who bear most caregiving responsibilities, limiting their participation in the workforce, contributing to the local affordability crisis, and affecting economic stability for families across Waterloo Region; and Whereas Whereas the provincial funding model does not provide sufficient local flexibility to respond to emerging needs and opportunities, even though this flexibility could allow operators to open additional spaces faster, and could allow operators to better support children with special needs and families eligible for fee subsidy; and Whereas several provinces and territories across Canada have already reached or are publicly reporting success in reaching regulated child-care fees of approximately $10-a-day or less under the Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care (CWELCC) program, including Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, and the territories such as Nunavut and Yukon, while Quebec contributes approximately $2.76 billion annually to sustain its long-established $10-a-day child-care system, demonstrating that meaningful and sustained provincial investment is essential for affordability, access, stability, and long-term success in early learning and child care; and Whereas the Province of Ontario recently added $276 million in childcare funding, an amount that is not proportional to the scale of unmet need nor comparable to the level of federal investment that has enabled the CWELCC system; and Whereas interest in operating licensed childcare significantly exceeds the provincially funded growth allocation, with many qualified operators unable to receive approval due to insufficient provincial funding; and Whereas the Region of Waterloo’s childcare system operates with 99.6% utilization of CWELCC infant, toddler, and preschool spaces, illustrating a system at full capacity with no room to absorb further demand without enhanced provincial investment. Therefore Be It Resolved That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo: Formally advocate to the Province of Ontario and the Minister of Education for substantial additional CWELCC funding to address the Region’s rapidly growing population including the thousands of children who are part of this growth and to address the current waitlist of 14,000 children and persistent historic underfunding. Request the Province provide greater local flexibility in funding , to enable faster, more efficient growth, and to respond to demonstrated community needs, including for children with special needs and families eligible for fee subsidy. Call on the Province to match the level of commitment shown by the federal government , acknowledging that the recent $276 million provincial contribution is insufficient relative to both the need and the federal investment driving the CWELCC system. Emphasize that insufficient provincial investment worsens gender inequities , contributes to the affordability crisis facing families, and limits women’s economic participation contrary to the goals of a strong, inclusive provincial economy. Request that the Province recognize Waterloo Region’s unique pressures as a large, growing Region with rural and urban centres and provide targeted, needs-based funding to the region that reflects its demographic growth, labour market importance, and the current inequities in childcare access. Direct the Regional Chair to communicate this motion to: The Premier of Ontario; The Minister of Education; Local MPs; Local MPPs; The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO); and The Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM).

motions.item_title: EES-WAS-26-001, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint Update
motions.text: Whereas in late November 2025, through on-going work and updates to the Water Supply Strategy, Regional staff have identified a water capacity constraint within the Mannheim Service Area, which supplies water to Kitchener, Waterloo, and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich, and Wilmot and Whereas a Technical Team has been meeting and working diligently since that time to research, understand and address these infrastructure challenges, and Whereas the Region of Waterloo staff on an ongoing basis monitors, maintains and updates an annual Asset Management Plan and Master Plans for all regional information including regional water and wastewater infrastructure and Whereas the Asset Management Plan “describes the replacement value and physical condition of the Region’ s asset portfolio” and this information is utilized to predict when renewals and repairs will likely be needed’, and Whereas the 2025 Asset Management Plan includes an Asset Condition profile of Water and Wastewater Services (see Appendix A, Figure A.1 of that report), Levels of Service information, a Drinking Water Quality Management System, Expenditure Forecasts and other aspects of the system all of which are all designed and used to ‘…manage risk to the water supply system by identifying possible hazards, assigning risk scores and identifying procedures, process objectives and preventative measures to help assess and mitigate risk to the environment.” and Whereas housing and employment developments currently in progress and scheduled to begin or to be completed in 2026 and developments being planned within the next 5 years require information as soon as possible regarding the short, medium and long-term plans for repairing the regional water and wastewater infrastructure, Whereas although the Report EES-WAS-26-001indicates that “a more fulsome impact of the capacity issue to the 2026 operating and capital budget is anticipated to be available late Q1 2026”, there is pressing need for area municipalities and the development community to understand the repairs needed and the timelines involved, Therefore be it resolved that the timeline for a preliminary list of the short, medium and long-term plans for the necessary infrastructure repairs be made publicly available before the end of January 2026 rather than in late Q1 2026.

motions.item_title: EES-WAS-26-001, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint Update
motions.text: Whereas in late November 2025, through on-going work and updates to the Water Supply Strategy, Regional staff have identified a water capacity constraint within the Mannheim Service Area, which supplies water to Kitchener, Waterloo, and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich, and Wilmot and Whereas a Technical Team has been meeting and working diligently since that time to research, understand and address these infrastructure challenges, and Whereas the Report EES-WAS-26-001indicates that ‘…several factors and observations led technical staff to reassess how remaining water capacity was being monitored including “a plateauing of conservation efforts…” and Whereas the water conservation efforts referred to in the report do not include the breadth of water conservation opportunities available to municipalities, homeowners, businesses, property owners, property managers and property developers which include but are not limited to, for example, natural assets – more trees, native plants, floodplain protection – the installation of green infrastructure, the adoption of greywater systems, rainwater capture for personal watering, smart irrigation systems, models for more sustainable water practices and an understanding of how technology and smart metering and data analytics can increase water conservation, and Whereas municipalities like the Region of Waterloo and other municipalities including area municipalities have the opportunity to provide leadership and direction with robust water conservation policy(ies) and appropriate regulations to support water conservation efforts, and Whereas water conservation efforts are required in tandem with the necessary infrastructure repairs and sourcing of new wells in order to ensure a robust water supply now and in the future, Therefore Be It Resolved that staff are directed to report back by the end of Q2 June 2026 with water conservation policy options for the Sustainability, Infrastructure and Development Committee’s and Regional Council’s consideration and Further that input from relevant community partners including but not limited to Reep Green Solutions, Sustainable Waterloo Region, Build Urban, the Waterloo Region Homebuilders Association, the Grand River Conservation Authority, Grand River Environmental Network and area municipalities is sought and included in the water conservation policy options proposed.

motions.item_title: EES-WAS-26-001, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint Update
motions.text: That Region of Waterloo staff make available to area municipalities, no later than end of January, all raw data that informed and encompasses the Agile Water Supply Peer Review and Assessment Report, and also report to Council by January 28 about also making that data available to industry and other community partners thereafter. Further that in sharing the data and existing information, details also be provided of all budget approved and other planned infrastructure works, along with their respective capacity gains, and associated timing to be brought online for capacity purposes.

motions.item_title: EES-WAS-26-001, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint Update
motions.text: THAT Regional staff be directed to provide a clear written definition of what activities are currently paused or restricted, including but not limited to servicing agreements, allocations, registrations, redevelopment scenarios, and planning approvals, no later than 12:00 p.m. on Friday, January 16, 2026, to: Regional Council, Area Municipal Councils, and the public; AND THAT Regional staff be further directed to report back to Council no later than Feb. 10, 2026 with a decision-ready information package related to the Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint, including: a) updated water supply and demand calculations using the revised methodology, including key assumptions and sensitivity testing under multiple resiliency buffer scenarios; b) a summary of interim operational and/or engineering measures considered to mitigate capacity constraints, including feasibility, estimated costs, regulatory requirements, and indicative timelines; c) an update of how the Region intends to address and resolve water supply capacity constraints while respecting the planning authority of Area Municipalities, including: how Regional water and wastewater infrastructure planning, investment, and operational decisions will support Area Municipalities in carrying out their legislated land use planning responsibilities; how growth-related servicing decisions will be aligned with approved Area Municipal official plans and provincial planning policy, rather than used as a mechanism to direct or prioritize growth outcomes; and what actions the Region will take, within its jurisdiction, to address system capacity and reliability so that Area Municipalities are able to proceed with planning and development in accordance with provincial legislation; d) a detailed workplan identifying specific dates and milestones, rather than quarter-based timelines, for further analysis, decisions, and recommendations requiring Council consideration; e) clear identification of matters requiring Council direction versus those within administrative authority. AND FURTHER THAT Regional staff be directed to bring forward a communications plan that includes public messaging, stakeholder outreach plans, or external communications related to the Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint for Council review and approval in advance of release or implementation, recognizing that: the matter has significant policy, economic, growth, and inter-municipal implications; such communications reflect Council direction and Council accountability; and this issue extends beyond routine administrative communications.

motions.item_title: EES-WAS-26-001, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint Update
motions.text: * Withdrew via unanimous consent * THAT Regional staff be directed to prepare an inventory and impact assessment of active and pending Ontario Permits to Take Water (PTTWs) that draw from groundwater sources within the Region of Waterloo and/or from connected aquifers within the broader watershed, including those located outside Regional boundaries; AND THAT the assessment include: a) the purpose, permitted volumes, and term of each identified permit; b) the relationship, if any, between those takings and Regional municipal water supply systems, including the Mannheim Service Area; c) an assessment of cumulative impacts on groundwater availability using the Region’s revised water capacity methodology; and d) identification of any permits that may warrant enhanced scrutiny, mitigation measures, or engagement with the Province in order to protect municipal drinking water security; AND THAT staff report back in open session by end of Q2 2026 with findings and recommended next steps, including potential advocacy or coordination with the Province of Ontario.

Complete application(s) to the Council of The Regional Municipality of Waterloo, as may be required from time to time, for approval to expropriate land, which is required for improvements to Fischer Hallman Road between Bleams Road and Plains Road, and described as follows: Temporary Easement – Grading: The right and easement, being a temporary easement in gross, for the free and unobstructed, right, interest and easement terminating, for the subject properties set out below, on the 31st day of December 2028, for itself, its successors and assigns, and anyone authorized by it, on, over, under and through the following property for the purposes of excavation, construction, installation, replacement, alteration, grading, and landscaping as required in connection with the improvements to Fischer Hallman Road between Bleams Road and Plains Road, and all related improvements, and works ancillary thereto and for such purposes, the free, unimpeded and unobstructed access to the lands at all times by employees, agents, contractors, workers and anyone authorized by it, and vehicles, supplies and equipment at all times and for all purposes and things necessary for or incidental to the exercise and enjoyment of the right and easement: Part of Lot 153, German Company Tract, being Part 1 on 58R-22431, City of Kitchener, part of PIN 22728-0960, (Part of Vacant Land, Fischer Hallman Road, Kitchener); Part of Lot 158, German Company Tract, being Part 7 on 58R-19936, City of Kitchener, part of PIN 22607-2288, (945 Huron Road, Kitchener); Part of Lot 5, Registrar’s Compiled Plan 1471, being Parts 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 on 58R-19942, City of Kitchener, part of PIN 22607-2322, (1340 Fischer Hallman Road, Kitchener); Part of Lot 6, Registrar’s Compiled Plan 1471, being Part 1 on 58R-19941, City of Kitchener, part of PIN 22607-2454, (Part of Vacant Land, Fischer Hallman Road, Kitchener); and Part of Lot 156, German Company Tract, being Part 3 on 58R-19941, City of Kitchener, part of PIN 22607-2317, (1548 Fischer Hallman Road, Kitchener) Serve notices of the above applications(s) required by the Expropriations Act (the “Act”); Forward to the Chief Inquiry Officer any requests for a hearing that may be received within the time prescribed by the Act; Attend, with appropriate Regional staff, at any hearing that may be scheduled; Discontinue expropriation proceedings or any part thereof, in respect of the above described lands, or any part thereof, upon the registration on title of the required documentation to complete a transaction whereby the required interests in the lands are conveyed or if otherwise deemed appropriate in the opinion of the Commissioner of Engineering and Environmental Services and the Regional Solicitor; and Do all things necessary and proper to be done and report thereon to Regional Council in due course. Whereas in late November 2025, through on-going work and updates to the Water Supply Strategy, Regional staff have identified a water capacity constraint within the Mannheim Service Area, which supplies water to Kitchener, Waterloo, and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich, and Wilmot and Whereas a Technical Team has been meeting and working diligently since that time to research, understand and address these infrastructure challenges, and Whereas the Region of Waterloo staff on an ongoing basis monitors, maintains and updates an annual Asset Management Plan and Master Plans for all regional information including regional water and wastewater infrastructure and Whereas the Asset Management Plan “describes the replacement value and physical condition of the Region’ s asset portfolio” and this information is utilized to predict when renewals and repairs will likely be needed’, and Whereas the 2025 Asset Management Plan includes an Asset Condition profile of Water and Wastewater Services (see Appendix A, Figure A.1 of that report), Levels of Service information, a Drinking Water Quality Management System, Expenditure Forecasts and other aspects of the system all of which are all designed and used to ‘…manage risk to the water supply system by identifying possible hazards, assigning risk scores and identifying procedures, process objectives and preventative measures to help assess and mitigate risk to the environment.” And Whereas housing and employment developments currently in progress and scheduled to begin or to be completed in 2026 and developments being planned within the next 5 years require information as soon as possible regarding the short, medium and long-term plans for repairing the regional water and wastewater infrastructure, Whereas although the Report EES-WAS-26-001indicates that “a more fulsome impact of the capacity issue to the 2026 operating and capital budget is anticipated to be available late Q1 2026”, there is pressing need for area municipalities and the development community to understand the repairs needed and the timelines involved, Therefore be it resolved that the timeline for a preliminary list of the short, medium and long-term plans for the necessary infrastructure repairs be made publicly available before the end of January 2026 rather than in late Q1 2026. Whereas in late November 2025, through on-going work and updates to the Water Supply Strategy, Regional staff have identified a water capacity constraint within the Mannheim Service Area, which supplies water to Kitchener, Waterloo, and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich, and Wilmot and Whereas a Technical Team has been meeting and working diligently since that time to research, understand and address these infrastructure challenges, and Whereas the Report EES-WAS-26-001indicates that ‘…several factors and observations led technical staff to reassess how remaining water capacity was being monitored including “a plateauing of conservation efforts…” and Whereas the water conservation efforts referred to in the report do not include the breadth of water conservation opportunities available to municipalities, homeowners, businesses, property owners, property managers and property developers which include but are not limited to, for example, natural assets – more trees, native plants, floodplain protection – the installation of green infrastructure, the adoption of greywater systems, rainwater capture for personal watering, smart irrigation systems, models for more sustainable water practices and an understanding of how technology and smart metering and data analytics can increase water conservation, and Whereas municipalities like the Region of Waterloo and other municipalities including area municipalities have the opportunity to provide leadership and direction with robust water conservation policy(ies) and appropriate regulations to support water conservation efforts, and Whereas water conservation efforts are required in tandem with the necessary infrastructure repairs and sourcing of new wells in order to ensure a robust water supply now and in the future, Therefore Be It Resolved that staff are directed to report back by the end of Q2 June 2026 with water conservation policy options for the Sustainability, Infrastructure and Development Committee’s and Regional Council’s consideration and Further that input from relevant community partners including but not limited to Reep Green Solutions, Sustainable Waterloo Region, Build Urban, the Waterloo Region Homebuilders Association, the Grand River Conservation Authority, Grand River Environmental Network and area municipalities is sought and included in the water conservation policy options proposed. That Region of Waterloo staff make available to area municipalities, no later than end of January, all raw data that informed and encompasses the Agile Water Supply Peer Review and Assessment Report, and also report to Council by January 28 about also making that data available to industry and other community partners thereafter. Further that in sharing the data and existing information, details also be provided of all budget approved and other planned infrastructure works, along with their respective capacity gains, and associated timing to be brought online for capacity purposes. That Regional staff report to the Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee in February 2026 on the types of developments and applications subject to Regional advisory comments.

motions.item_title: EES-WIM-26-001, Preliminary Water Capacity Constraint Solutions and Associated Resource Needs
motions.text: WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo has identified significant water supply capacity constraints within the Mannheim Service Area through its Water Supply Strategy update and associated third party technical review; and WHEREAS the Region’s existing methodology for determining remaining water supply capacity requires updating to reflect operational constraints, hydrological realities, and the need to maintain an operational resiliency buffer; and WHEREAS the Region’s current policy permits consideration of future, unbuilt service capacity where: A capacity expansion project is imminent and included in the first five years of the Region’s 10year capital forecast, A sound technical basis exists for the anticipated capacity (supported by an Environmental Assessment, master plan, or equivalent engineering analysis), and Area Municipal recommendations guide approvals, with no more than 50% of projected new capacity allocated in advance of completion; and WHEREAS the Region has developed a preliminary list of initiatives to restore and increase capacity within the Mannheim Service Area; and WHEREAS municipal and industry partners have identified the urgent need for a clear, transparent, Regionwide allocation approach to ensure consistent interpretation of capacity constraints and development impacts across all area municipalities; and WHEREAS Waterloo Region continues to be in a housing supply crisis, particularly for lower income individuals within Waterloo Region; and WHEREAS according to the 2019 labour force survey 24,300 people are employed in construction which could be at risk from a total development freeze THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That in accordance with Region’s long-standing policy, as outlined above, Region staff be directed to work with Area Municipalities on development applications and use up to fifty per cent of planned and unbuilt capacity coming on-line within the next 5 years to support development approvals and operational resiliency so that: the Region of Waterloo can continue to enter into servicing agreements and approve Form 1s for development applications that have been deemed as complete applications by Area Municipalities prior to December 4, 2025; and, Area Municipalities can continue with typical processing of all development applications that have been deemed complete applications by Area Municipalities prior to December 4, 2025; and,

motions.item_title: Councillor M. Rodrigues, Re: Road Safety Program
motions.text: WHEREAS the Road User Safety Program provides comprehensive, evidence-based solutions to reduce serious injuries and fatalities on Regional Roads, with an emphasis on reducing serious collisions involving vulnerable road users including in school zones; WHEREAS revenues from Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE) in school zones would have funded the Road Safety Reserve as a primary funding source for the Road User Safety Program; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Regional staff report to the Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee by Q2 2026 and following wind-down of the ASE program to: Establish how to allocate the remaining Road Safety Reserve balance to fund school zone road safety initiatives starting in 2026; and Provide options on how to fund the Road Safety Reserve in future years, including but not limited to sources from transportation user fees and redlight camera revenues.

motions.item_title: Councillor J. Gowing, Re: Bulky Item Collection Frequency Review
motions.text: That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff be directed to explore alternative service frequency models for the Region’s bulky item collection program, including: Monthly collection; Semi-monthly (every two months) collection; Semi-annual collection; And maintaining the current biweekly model as a baseline comparator. And that staff report back to Council with: A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of each model, including projected operational savings, fleet and staffing impacts, contract considerations, and administrative efficiencies. An assessment of environmental and community impacts , including potential changes to waste diversion, illegal dumping risks, and any required mitigation strategies. An analysis of resident experience implications , including accessibility and communication requirements. A recommended optimal scenario based on financial, operational, environmental, and community impacts. Options for phased implementation , pilot testing, or transition planning should Council consider changing the current service frequency.

motions.item_title: Councillor D. Craig, Re: Continued Election of Regional Chair
motions.text: Whereas the region of Waterloo has a long standing governance model in which the Regional Chair is elected by the voters of the entire region, providing a direct democratic mandate, And where as the Regional Chair presides over decisions affecting all residents of the Region of Waterloo, including taxation, growth management, housing, public health , policing and social services, And whereas, the direct election of the Regional Chair enhances accountability, transparency, and public confidence in regional decision making, And whereas, provincially appointed municipal roles reduce the local democratic choice and weaken the principle that municipal governments are creatures of local representation, not provincial discretion, And whereas, any change to the method of selecting the Regional Chair should respect local traditions and be undertaken only with the consent of the affected community, Therefore Be It Resolved That The Council of the Region of Waterloo formally requests the Province of Ontario to affirm and support the continued election of the Regional Chair by the voters of the Region of Waterloo, And that the province be requested not to impose or advance legislation that would replaced an elected chair with a provincially appointed position, And that the province be further requested to consult with the Region of Waterloo and its area municipalities prior to any proposed changes to the regional governance structure, And that a copy of this motion be forwarded to: The Premier of Ontario; The Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; The Minister of Finance; All members of Provincial Parliament representing Waterloo Region; and The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

motions.item_title: EES-WIM-26-003, Optimizing the Sustainable Use of Water Resources for Municipal Supply (1980 Policy on Water Taking - Wilmot Township)
motions.text: Motion Referred That Council temporarily suspend the 1980 Council Wilmot Water Take Policy, rather than revoke it, until the Region’s new Water Supply Strategy is completed and presented to Council in 2027; That Council formally review the status of the 1980 policy upon receipt of the Water Supply Strategy in 2027, prior to making any permanent determination respecting revocation; That upon initiation of any increased draw from Wilmot wells , staff provide regular public reporting to Regional Council and the public, at a minimum quarterly, including but not limited to: total volume of water being taken; peak flow data; well performance indicators; aquifer health and drawdown monitoring data; commentary on whether continued suspension remains appropriate based on observed conditions; That staff establish and implement a monitoring framework to collect and publicly report data regarding: neighbouring private wells; surface water systems; agricultural water supply conditions; and any observed correlations associated with increased regional draw; That staff provide Council and the public with a clear definition of “surplus water” as used in Regional staffs SID Feb. 10 report on the 1980 water take policy, including: the modelling methodology applied; growth and demand assumptions used; safety factors and contingency thresholds; and alignment with Provincial permitting requirements; That staff provide clarification regarding the basis of the current statement that Wilmot’s growth to 2051 will not be impacted , including: the population and employment forecasts being used; the land use assumptions underlying those forecasts; the infrastructure modelling methodology applied; and the treatment of post-2051 growth within long-term supply planning; That the forthcoming Water Supply Strategy clearly distinguish between water allocation assumptions for Wilmot’s planned residential and employment growth and any projected demand associated with the Region’s designated Mega Site , including: the range of potential end-user water demand scenarios being modelled for the mega site; the planning assumptions being used in the absence of a confirmed end user; and the implications of those assumptions for long-term regional water allocation and that the mega site water use is independent of the guaranteed allocations for Wilmot's planned growth as per their 2026 Official Plan

motions.item_title: Councillor J. Gowing, Protection of Existing Groundwater Supply and Wetlands
motions.text: That staff of the Region of Waterloo be directed to report back to Council alongside the Water Supply Strategy in 2027 or sooner on measures available to protect and preserve the Region’s existing groundwater supply and associated wetlands, recognizing current water capacity constraints, long-term asset management planning and recent provincial legislative changes, including: an assessment of the effectiveness of existing Regional policies, designations, and development controls in protecting groundwater recharge areas, source water protection zones, wetlands, and moraine lands that contribute to the Region’s current water supply, and identification of any gaps or vulnerabilities; an evaluation of how land-use change within recharge areas and wetlands may affect groundwater availability, long-term water security, and future infrastructure requirements under existing growth scenarios; identification of planning, policy, or regulatory tools currently available to the Region to strengthen protection of existing water supply sources within the constraints of Bill 23 and provincial housing and growth objectives; consideration of precautionary or interim risk-mitigation measures that could reduce further stress on existing groundwater systems while remaining compliant with provincial legislation; identification of opportunities for coordination with area municipalities and conservation authorities to improve alignment between source water protection science and land-use decision-making; options for the Region to advocate to the Provincial Government for a provincially enabled “Bluebelt” or similar legislative framework to provide permanent protection for critical groundwater recharge areas, wetlands, and moraine lands beyond municipal authority, including an assessment of potential implications for growth management and infrastructure planning. And that the report be presented for information and discussion purposes, without prejudice, to future policy direction of Council.

motions.item_title: Councillor J. Gowing, Re: Bulky Item Collection Frequency Review
motions.text: That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff be directed to explore alternative service frequency models for the Region’s bulky item collection program, including: Monthly collection; Semi-monthly (every two months) collection; Semi-annual collection; And maintaining the current biweekly model as a baseline comparator. And that staff report back to Council by September 2026 including information on the Christmas Tree Bulk Item. with: A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of each model, including projected operational savings, fleet and staffing impacts, contract considerations, and administrative efficiencies. An assessment of environmental and community impacts , including potential changes to waste diversion, illegal dumping risks, and any required mitigation strategies. An analysis of resident experience implications , including accessibility and communication requirements. A recommended optimal scenario based on financial, operational, environmental, and community impacts. Options for phased implementation , pilot testing, or transition planning should Council consider changing the current service frequency.

motions.item_title: Councillor B. Vrbanovic, Water Capacity Constraint Solutions
motions.text: WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo has identified water supply capacity constraints within the Mannheim Service Area through its Water Supply Strategy update and associated third party technical review; and WHEREAS the Region’s existing methodology for determining remaining water supply capacity has been updated to reflect operational constraints, hydrological realities, and the need to maintain an operational resiliency buffer; and WHEREAS the Region has already established a risk-based approach to provide allocation of future unbuilt water and wastewater service capacity to enable growth (example: plans of subdivision) where the following criteria has been met: A capacity expansion project is imminent and included in the first five years of the Region’s 10year capital forecast, A sound technical basis exists for the anticipated capacity (supported by an Environmental Assessment, master plan, or equivalent engineering analysis), and Area Municipal recommendations guide approvals, with no more than 50% of projected new capacity allocated in advance of completion; and WHEREAS the Region has developed a preliminary list of initiatives to restore and increase capacity within the Mannheim Service Area; and WHEREAS municipal and industry partners have identified the urgent need for a clear, transparent, Regionwide allocation approach to ensure consistent interpretation of capacity constraints and development impacts across all area municipalities; and WHEREAS Waterloo Region continues to be in a housing supply crisis, particularly for lower income individuals within Waterloo Region; and WHEREAS according to the 2019 labour force survey 24,300 people are employed in construction which could be at risk. THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Region staff be directed to work with Area Municipalities on a risk-based approach to advance the allocation of up to fifty per cent of planned and unbuilt capacity coming on-line within the next 5 years to support development approvals, in conjunction with restoring sustainable operating rates, and the minimum operational resiliency, consistent with the Region’s long-standing practice. That Regional staff work with Area Municipalities to develop and implement an enhanced water conservation program, including possible regulatory, pricing and incentive-based measures, to both mitigate peak system demands year-round and especially from May 1 – September 30 in order to enable restored and new water supply capacity to come online in parallel with continued development approvals as outlined in Recommendation 1.

motions.item_title: Administration and Finance Committee - February 10, 2026
motions.text: The Administration and Finance Committee recommends as follows: 1. That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct Facilities staff to explore the development of a Facilities Strategic Plan focused on the following five components: A complete inventory of all corporate facilities, including current usage, functional capacity, and condition; An analysis of operating and maintenance requirements and associated costs across all corporate facilities; A five- to ten-year capital outlook identifying required investments, lifecycle needs, and projected financial impacts; A review of accommodation standards and policies to support facilities planning and a demand analysis to clarify space needs; An evaluation of optimization opportunities, including consolidation, repurposing, or alternative service delivery options to ensure efficient and cost-effective use of corporate space; And that staff report back to Council with the findings, options, and recommended next steps. 2. The Council of the Region of Waterloo formally requests the Province of Ontario to affirm and support the continued election of the Regional Chair by the voters of the Region of Waterloo or appointed by Region of Waterloo Council, And that the province be requested not to impose or advance legislation that would replace an elected chair with a provincially appointed position, And that the province be further requested to consult with the Region of Waterloo and its area municipalities prior to any proposed changes to the regional governance structure, And that a copy of this motion be forwarded to: The Premier of Ontario; The Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; The Minister of Finance; All members of Provincial Parliament representing Waterloo Region; and The Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Region staff be directed to work with Area Municipalities on a risk-based approach to advance the allocation of up to fifty per cent of planned and unbuilt capacity coming on-line within the next 5 years to support development approvals, in conjunction with restoring sustainable operating rates, and the minimum operational resiliency, consistent with the Region’s long-standing practice. That Regional staff work with Area Municipalities to develop and implement an enhanced water conservation program, including possible regulatory, pricing and incentive-based measures, to both mitigate peak system demands year-round and especially from May 1 – September 30 in order to enable restored and new water supply capacity to come online in parallel with continued development approvals as outlined in Recommendation 1.

motions.item_title: Councillor D. Craig
motions.text: Whereas the Region of Waterloo is experiencing increasing constraints and uncertainty related to municipal water supply and capacity; and Whereas residents and the development industry have raised concerns regarding water sustainability, growth pressures and the availability of clear and transparent public information related to long term water planning; and Whereas a previous council motion authorized only staff level discussions with representatives of the Waterloo Home Builders Association, Build Urban, and the Grand Valley Construction Association regarding water supply constraints in an initial technical exchange; and Whereas water supply planning is a fundamental core public interest issue that requires direct engagement by Regional Council to ensure transparency, accountability and informed decision making. Therefore, be it resolved: That Regional Council direct staff to convene a one day working session involving regional council, relevant regional staff and invited representatives of the development industry including the Waterloo Home Builders association, Build Urban and the Grand Valley Construction Association to provide a comprehensive briefing on the Region’s water supply; and The working session be educational and informational in nature inviting commentary from both council and the development industry on water sustainability, growth pressures and the possibility of new guidelines on the staging of development; and Staff report back to council following the working session with a summary of key information presented, suggestions from the development industry on the staging of approvals and further recommended next steps for council.

motions.item_title: Councillor J. Gowing
motions.text: WHEREAS the Province of Ontario regulates Permits to Take Water (PTTW) under the Ontario Water Resources Act; AND WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo relies primarily on groundwater for its municipal drinking water supply; AND WHEREAS provincial data indicates there are currently 108 active PTTWs within the Region of Waterloo, authorizing a combined maximum taking of approximately 1.01 billion litres per day; AND WHEREAS within the Mannheim Service Area, there are 65 active permits authorizing approximately 740 million litres per day, of which 22 municipal permits account for approximately 472 million litres per day and 43 private permits account for approximately 268 million litres per day; AND WHEREAS recent groundwater capacity constraints identified within the Mannheim Service Area highlight the need for a precautionary and cumulative aquifer-level review of permitted water takings; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT: The Region of Waterloo formally request that the Province of Ontario implement a temporary moratorium on the issuance or expansion of new private-sector Permits to Take Water within areas experiencing identified groundwater capacity constraints, including the Mannheim Service Area, until a cumulative aquifer-level impact review is completed; The Province undertake a regional cumulative groundwater impact assessment of all existing PTTWs within Waterloo Region, incorporating climate variability, drought resiliency, and projected population growth; The Province strengthen municipal engagement in the PTTW review process by requiring formal notification to affected municipalities of new, amended, or renewed PTTW applications; a defined municipal commenting period; and a written provincial response addressing municipal comments prior to final permit decisions; While the Province currently publishes a quarterly Permit to Take Water dataset, proactive notification and supporting documentation be provided directly to affected municipalities at the time of application submission and final decision; Enhanced annual public reporting be provided outlining permitted daily volumes by municipality; municipal versus private breakdowns; and aggregate actual annual takings compared to permitted maximums; This resolution be forwarded to the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks; the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing; local Members of Provincial Parliament; and the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

motions.item_title: Councillor C. Huinink Motion Re: Accessibility Standards
motions.text: WHEREAS over their lifespan most Ontarians will encounter some form of accessibility barriers in the built environment and the design of public spaces, AND WHEREAS the Ontario Building Code establishes only a minimum level of accessibility for buildings and therefore does not presently meet the accessibility needs of all people, AND WHEREAS accessibility in the built environment should be improved by integrating standards into the Code that promote meaningful access of buildings and sites for people with a range of accessibility requirements including vision, hearing, neurodiversity, and mobility, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT The Regional Municipality of Waterloo requests that the Province of Ontario incorporate the latest accessibility standards established by the Canadian Standards Association (CSA) into the Provincial Building Code to ensure that all new construction of public spaces in Ontario meets accessibility standards, and that the provincial government commits to achieving the Rick Hansen Foundation Accessibility Certification (RHFAC) gold certification on all its newly constructed buildings. And further that a copy of this motion be sent to: • The Honourable Doug Ford, Premier of Ontario • The Honourable Rob Flack, Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing • Local and area MPs, MPPs and Heads of Council • The Association of Municipalities of Ontario • Ontario’s Big City Mayors and • Mayors and Regional Chairs of Ontario

motions.text: Whereas, the Region of Waterloo is responsible for the long term planning, management and reporting of essential water infrastructure capacity, And whereas, recent reporting indicates a significant shortfall in water capacity that undermines previous projections and communications provided to Council and the public over the past five years, And whereas, the capacity issue has immediate and detrimental impacts on economic development and municipal planning, And whereas, an objective, transparent and comprehensive understanding as to why this occurred is important in restoring public trust and preventing future occurrences, Therefore be it resolved, That council directs the CAO to retain a qualified independent third-party firm to investigate the region’s water capacity reporting and communicating processes prior to 2026 And that the review examine: when capacity concerns were first identified, what internal reporting occurred and at what levels, whether existing thresholds or triggers for escalation to council notification are adequate, whether governance, communication or resource gaps contributed to any delay, And that, the report back to Regional council include: A clear timeline of events and decision points with findings on accountability and process gaps, And recommendations to ensure early notification of future infrastructure risks, And any recommended policy, governance or procedural changes to strengthen transparency and Council oversight. motions.item_title: EES-WIM-26-003, Optimizing the Sustainable Use of Water Resources for Municipal Supply (1980 Policy on Water Taking - Wilmot Township)
motions.text: Motion Referred That Council temporarily suspend the 1980 Council Wilmot Water Take Policy, rather than revoke it, until the Region’s new Water Supply Strategy is completed and presented to Council in 2027; That Council formally review the status of the 1980 policy upon receipt of the Water Supply Strategy in 2027, prior to making any permanent determination respecting revocation; That upon initiation of any increased draw from Wilmot wells, staff provide regular public reporting to Regional Council and the public, at a minimum quarterly, including but not limited to: total volume of water being taken; peak flow data; well performance indicators; aquifer health and drawdown monitoring data; commentary on whether continued suspension remains appropriate based on observed conditions; That staff establish and implement a monitoring framework to collect and publicly report data regarding: neighbouring private wells; surface water systems; agricultural water supply conditions; and any observed correlations associated with increased regional draw; That staff provide Council and the public with a clear definition of “surplus water” as used in Regional staff's SID Feb. 10 report on the 1980 water take policy, including: the modelling methodology applied; growth and demand assumptions used; safety factors and contingency thresholds; and alignment with Provincial permitting requirements; That staff provide clarification regarding the basis of the current statement that Wilmot’s growth to 2051 will not be impacted, including: the population and employment forecasts being used; the land use assumptions underlying those forecasts; the infrastructure modelling methodology applied; and the treatment of post-2051 growth within long-term supply planning; That the forthcoming Water Supply Strategy clearly distinguish between water allocation assumptions for Wilmot’s planned residential and employment growth and any projected demand associated with the Region’s designated Mega Site, including: the range of potential end-user water demand scenarios being modelled for the mega site; the planning assumptions being used in the absence of a confirmed end user; and the implications of those assumptions for long-term regional water allocation and that the mega site water use is independent of the guaranteed allocations for Wilmot's planned growth as per their 2026 Official Plan And that prior to implementation, Council be provided written confirmation that all applicable provincial permits and regulatory approvals required to support the increased water taking have been obtained

motions.text: WHEREAS the Province of Ontario regulates Permits to Take Water (PTTW) under the Ontario Water Resources Act; AND WHEREAS the Region of Waterloo relies primarily on groundwater for its municipal drinking water supply; AND WHEREAS provincial data indicates there are currently 108 active PTTWs within the Region of Waterloo, authorizing a combined maximum taking of approximately 1.01 billion litres per day; AND WHEREAS within the Mannheim Service Area municipalities (City of Kitchener, City of Waterloo, Township of Woolwich, and Township of Wilmot ), there are 65 active permits authorizing approximately 740 million litres per day, of which 22 municipal permits account for approximately 472 million litres per day and 43 private permits account for approximately 268 million litres per day; AND WHEREAS recent groundwater capacity constraints identified within the Mannheim Service Area highlight the need for a precautionary and cumulative aquifer-level review of private permitted water takings to prevent the risk of interference to existing municipal and private water supplies, and to safeguard groundwater resources for both the natural environment and potential future use for municipal water supply; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT: The Region of Waterloo formally request the Province of Ontario: implement a temporary moratorium on the issuance of new or expansion of existing private-sector Permits to Take Water within areas of the Region of Waterloo experiencing identified groundwater capacity constraints, including the Mannheim Service Area, until completion of the Region’s Water Supply Strategy Update; continue municipal engagement in the PTTW review process by providing formal notification to affected municipalities of new, amended, or renewed PTTW applications; a defined municipal commenting period; and a written provincial response addressing municipal comments prior to final permit decisions; and Whilethe Province currently publishes a quarterly Permit to Take Water dataset, require proactive notification and supporting documentation be provided directly to the Region of Waterloo at the time of application submission and final decision.

motions.item_title: Notice of Motion
motions.text: Whereas the Region of Waterloo’s Community Safety and Well-Being Plan, developed under the requirements of the Community Safety and Policing Act, identifies systemic racism, hate, and discrimination as critical risk factors impacting community safety, belonging, and well-being; And whereas the display of a noose is widely recognized as a symbol of racial terror, violence, and intimidation, particularly against Black communities, rooted in the history of anti-Black racism; And whereas symbols of hate, when displayed publicly, contribute to fear, trauma, and exclusion, and undermine the Region’s commitments to equity, inclusion, and proactive prevention within its Community Safety and Well-Being Plan; And whereas the Government of Canada has introduced Bill C-9 to strengthen tools to address hate-motivated offences, including provisions related to the public display of certain hate symbols; And whereas the current draft of Bill C-9 does not explicitly include the noose as a prohibited symbol, despite its well-documented use as an instrument of racial intimidation and its direct relevance to community safety and well-being outcomes; And whereas addressing hate symbols through federal legislation complements municipal efforts by strengthening upstream prevention, reducing harm, and supporting safer, more inclusive communities; Therefore be it resolved that: The Regional Municipality of Waterloo formally request that the Government of Canada amend Bill C-9 to explicitly include the noose as a prohibited hate symbol within the legislation; The Regional Chair be directed to send correspondence to the Hon. MP Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada, local Members of Parliament, and relevant federal committees conveying this request, including the Senate of Canada, noting its alignment with the Region’s Community Safety and Well-Being Plan priorities; This motion be circulated to all Ontario municipalities, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM), and the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) for endorsement and support as a measure that strengthens community safety and well-being across jurisdictions.

motions.item_title: Deferred Motion - 1980 Policy on Water Taking - Wilmot Township
motions.text: That Council temporarily suspend the 1980 Council Wilmot Water Take Policy, rather than revoke it, until the Region’s new Water Supply Strategy is completed and presented to Council in 2027; That Council formally review the status of the 1980 policy upon receipt of the Water Supply Strategy in 2027, prior to making any permanent determination respecting revocation; That upon initiation of any increased draw from Wilmot wells, staff provide regular public reporting to Regional Council and the public, at a minimum quarterly, including but not limited to: total volume of water being taken; peak flow data; well performance indicators; aquifer health and drawdown monitoring data; commentary on whether continued suspension remains appropriate based on observed conditions; That staff establish and implement a monitoring framework to collect and publicly report data regarding: neighbouring private wells; surface water systems; agricultural water supply conditions; and any observed correlations associated with increased regional draw; That staff provide Council and the public with a clear definition of “surplus water” as used in Regional staff's SID Feb. 10 report on the 1980 water take policy, including: the modelling methodology applied; growth and demand assumptions used; safety factors and contingency thresholds; and alignment with Provincial permitting requirements; That staff provide clarification regarding the basis of the current statement that Wilmot’s growth to 2051 will not be impacted, including: the population and employment forecasts being used; the land use assumptions underlying those forecasts; the infrastructure modelling methodology applied; and the treatment of post-2051 growth within long-term supply planning; That the forthcoming Water Supply Strategy clearly distinguish between water allocation assumptions for Wilmot’s planned residential and employment growth and any projected demand associated with the Region’s designated Mega Site, including: the range of potential end-user water demand scenarios being modelled for the mega site; the planning assumptions being used in the absence of a confirmed end user; and the implications of those assumptions for long-term regional water allocation and that the mega site water use is independent of the guaranteed allocations for Wilmot's planned growth as per their 2026 Official Plan And that prior to implementation, Council be provided written confirmation that all applicable provincial permits and regulatory approvals required to support the increased water taking have been obtained

motions.item_title: Councillor J. Gowing
motions.text: As Amended: Municipal Housing Corporation – Strategic Review WHEREAS the Region continues to experience increasing housing pressures, including chronic homelessness and sustained demand for emergency shelter services; AND WHEREAS expanding access to permanent supportive and affordable housing is a key component of improving housing stability and reducing long-term reliance on emergency systems; AND WHEREAS municipalities across Ontario have established Municipal Housing Corporations as strategic tools to support the development, delivery, and long-term management of housing; AND WHEREAS such a model may provide the Region with additional capacity to deliver housing, leverage external funding, and support long-term financial sustainability; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT: Staff be directed to report back to Community and Health Services Committee by Q2 2027 on the feasibility and potential role of establishing a Municipal Housing Corporation for the Region. That the review consider how such a corporation could support a phased approach to housing delivery , including an initial focus on supportive housing, Waterloo Region Housing Revitalization Plan priority projects and broader opportunities for affordable and mixed-income housing over time. That staff report on governance, financial, and operational considerations , including potential approaches to capitalization, partnerships, and long-term asset management. That the report identify potential benefits, risks, and implementation considerations , including opportunities to leverage federal and provincial housing funding programs. AND FURTHER THAT: The review include consideration of how such a model could contribute to improved housing outcomes, including reducing chronic homelessness and pressures on emergency shelter systems.

motions.item_title: Councillor C. James
motions.text: WHEREAS elected officials are required to attend Council, committee, and other official meetings that frequently occur during evenings, weekends, or outside standard child care and caregiving hours; and WHEREAS the lack of affordable, flexible childcare and caregiving options is a documented barrier to participation in municipal governance, disproportionately impacting women, single parents, individuals with caregiving responsibilities for children or elder family members, and others with dependent care obligations, including persons with disabilities; and WHEREAS in Ontario, there is no standardized legislative framework supporting caregiving leave for municipal elected officials, and no province-wide mechanism to recognize caregiving-related interruptions as a protected status in elected office, resulting in a gap in supports for those balancing public service with caregiving responsibilities; and WHEREAS the removal of systemic barriers to seeking and holding elected office is essential to ensuring municipal councils are representative of the communities they serve; and WHEREAS a growing number of Canadian municipalities have adopted reimbursement-based policies (not allowances) for childcare and caregiving expenses incurred by elected officials in the course of their official duties, including the City of Sarnia, Ontario, and municipalities in Alberta such as Banff and Okotoks; and WHEREAS such policies are structured as cost-recovery mechanisms that reimburse actual, reasonable expenses directly related to the performance of official municipal responsibilities and are distinct from remuneration or personal benefits. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT: Council directs staff to prepare and bring forward amendments to the elected officials’ expense reimbursement policy to explicitly include reimbursement for reasonable and necessary childcare and/or caregiving expenses (including elder care) incurred while performing official duties at Council, committee, and other approved municipal business; and Council further directs staff to report back with a proposed policy framework that includes: A jurisdictional scan of comparable Canadian municipal policies, including the City of Sarnia and municipalities in Alberta such as Banff and Okotoks; and A review of legislative authority and legal considerations under the Municipal Act, 2001 and applicable expense by-laws; Clearly defined eligibility criteria, documentation requirements, cost controls, and transparency and accountability measures; and A detailed analysis of the financial implications. Council directs that, upon approval, the finalized policy be formally shared with Area Municipalities, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM) as a best practice to support inclusive and representative local governance.

motions.item_title: N. Salonen motion from budget re: WRHN special levy
motions.text: Whereas the Province of Ontario requires municipalities to contribute a local share toward major hospital capital projects, and the forthcoming Waterloo Region Health Network (WRHN) hospital project is anticipated to require one of the largest municipal contributions in the Region’s history; Whereas early estimates indicate that the Region’s required local share will be in the multiple hundreds of millions, and this magnitude of investment will require long-term, disciplined financial planning; Whereas the Region of Waterloo must balance many competing and necessary capital priorities, and failing to begin reserving funds now would require significant future tax impacts or the deferral of other essential regional projects; Whereas establishing a dedicated, interest-bearing reserve fund enables the Region to gradually and responsibly accumulate contributions over multiple budget cycles, mitigating the need for sudden or unsustainable fiscal adjustments once the provincial approval process is finalized; Therefore be it resolved that: Council establish a Special Hospital Local Share Levy equivalent to 0.5% of the annual tax-supported budget, beginning in the 2026 fiscal year. All revenues collected through this Special Levy be directed to a newly created “Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund,” to be invested in accordance with the Region’s investment policy to allow funds to grow over time. The Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund be used exclusively for the municipal local share contribution required for the future WRHN hospital project and subsequently agreed upon Cambridge Hospital projects. Staff be directed to report annually during the budget process on the balance, growth, and projected trajectory of the Special Hospital Local Share Reserve Fund to ensure transparency and enable long-term planning. That staff bring back before budget 2027 the local share amount confirmed by the Province to Council, or continued suggestion for 2027 levy amount.

motions.item_title: Councillor D. Craig
motions.text: Whereas: The historic community off Blair Village is experiencing increasing traffic volumes, congestion ands safety concerns, And whereas, the broader corridor including Shantz Hill, Fountain Street and King Street is experiencing congestion, extended queuing and slower travel times, And whereas traffic conditions in these areas are interconnected with congestion delays that are having spillover effects and short cutting through adjacent neighbourhoods including Blair Village, And whereas ongoing residential and employment growth continues to place increasing pressure on this road network, And whereas concerns have been raised regarding road safety , pedestrian impacts, speeding and the impact on the heritage designated Blair Village, And whereas a coordinated system-wide analysis may be required to properly assess traffic operations, safety impacts and long term infrastructure needs across this corridor, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Regional Council direct staff through the“Integrated Mobility Plan” to initiate a review of traffic and safety encompassing Blair Village , Fountain Street, Shantz Hill Road, Fountain Street and the connections to King Street, And that the review include past studies on traffic volumes, turning movements , safety analysis, signal coordination and growth impacts, And that the review identify possible medium and long term solutions including operational improvements, roadway modifications and potential network changes, And that the review comment on past studies of a by-pass for the Blair Village and the possibility of an alternative by-pass that respects all the environmental issues of the surrounding area.

motions.item_title: Councillor N. Salonen
motions.text: WHEREAS residents who rely on private wells must have access to a fair, transparent, evidence-based, and resident-centred process when they experience groundwater interference that may be connected to Regional water-taking activities; AND WHEREAS the Region’s current Policy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints , revised in April 2015, provides for Regional staff to investigate complaints and provides that appeals are heard by the Commissioner of Transportation and Environmental Services (now interim Commissioner of Water Services and Wastewater Operations); AND WHEREAS prior to the 2015 policy change, groundwater interference appeals in the Region of Waterloo were heard through a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee, formerly known as the Regional Water Liaison Committee; AND WHEREAS residents have raised concerns that the current process does not provide sufficient independence, transparency, or meaningful appeal from staff determinations, particularly where the Region is both the operator of the municipal wells and the body responsible for investigating and deciding complaints related to those wells; AND WHEREAS other Ontario municipalities, including the City of Guelph, maintain a Well Interference Committee model to hear appeals where a resident is dissatisfied with the municipality’s investigation, resolution, or compensation related to municipal groundwater taking; AND WHEREAS the City of Guelph’s Well Interference Committee model provides for a committee to review staff investigations, hear directly from affected well owners, consider municipal pumping data and well information, and recommend restoration or additional restoration where appropriate; AND WHEREAS the purpose of any well interference process should be to restore an adequate and reliable water supply to affected residents, rather than to limit the Region’s response to a fixed compensation amount that may not reflect the actual cost of restoration; AND WHEREAS residents in multiple areas of the Region have raised concerns regarding groundwater interference associated with municipal pumping activities; AND WHEREAS public confidence in groundwater management is strengthened through transparent, evidence-based, and arms-length review processes; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff to bring forward a report and draft revised policy to the August 12, 2026 Special Council Water meeting to replace the current groundwater interference appeal process with a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee; AND THAT the revised policy and Terms of Reference be modelled on best practices from comparable municipal well interference appeal processes, including the City of Guelph model, and include the following: a) a mandate for the Committee to hear appeals from private well owners regarding groundwater interference complaints related to Regional water-taking activities; b) a process for the Committee to be convened where Regional staff determine that the Region is not responsible for a well interference complaint, where a resident is dissatisfied with the resolution offered, or where a resident is dissatisfied with the amount or form of compensation offered; c) a membership model that includes members of Regional Council and representatives from affected lower-tier municipalities, with consideration given to independent hydrogeological or technical expertise; d) a requirement that members hearing an appeal be independent from the staff responsible for the original investigation and recommendation; e) a process that allows affected residents to provide written materials, attend the hearing, present evidence, respond to staff findings, and answer questions from the Committee; f) a requirement that the Committee review all relevant information, including the location of the affected well relative to Regional wells, private well depth and water levels, municipal well details, municipal pumping data, water-level monitoring data, complaint history, investigation findings, and any mitigation measures taken to date; g) authority for the Committee to make recommendations to Regional Council respecting appropriate remedies, including temporary water supply, pump lowering, well deepening, new well drilling, connection to municipal water where feasible, abandonment of the old well where required, reimbursement of eligible costs, or other measures necessary to restore a reliable water supply; h) options to remove or revise the current $4,000 compensation limit where the evidence supports greater actual costs to restore an adequate water supply; i) options to ensure residents are not required to sign a full and final release of future claims before having access to a meaningful appeal process; j) enhanced public transparency respecting groundwater monitoring data, complaint tracking, investigation reporting, and Committee recommendations to Council, while protecting the personal information and privacy of affected residents; k) options for annual reporting to Council respecting the number, status, and resolution of groundwater interference complaints, trends, and mitigation measures undertaken by the Region; AND THAT staff include a transition provision allowing any resident who has submitted a groundwater interference complaint related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells since January 1, 2019, including residents who previously received a staff determination, compensation offer, denial, or release request, to request review through the new appeal process; AND THAT pending Council’s consideration of the revised policy, staff be directed not to require residents with active or unresolved complaints related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells to sign a full and final release as a condition of receiving temporary water support or emergency assistance; AND THAT staff report back with any legal, financial, staffing, procedural, privacy, and operational implications required to implement the revised process, including any amendments required to the current Policy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints or any related Regional policies.
